moduleTitle: Assigning and completing work for Business Architects
learningObjectives: Describe the business value of Pega's workflow automation features associated with routing and approvals.
Explain the importance of work groups in improving process efficiency.
Differentiate between the goal and deadline intervals relative to Service-Level Agreements.
Explain how urgency supports prioritization without guaranteeing timely completion.

elements.description: Routing assigns responsibility to configured users or queues using explicit destinations or conditions. Get Next Work separately selects suitable work using urgency, availability and skills; not every routing setting automatically computes the best available agent.

items: WORKLIST — Assignments routed to a SPECIFIC user (operator) to work individually
WORK QUEUE — a SHARED queue for a team/Work Group; any qualified member can pull and complete the work

elements.description: App Studio supports current user, specific user, Work Queue and business-logic routing. Business conditions can choose different user/queue destinations; Get Next Work selection also evaluates urgency, availability and skills.

elements.text: A Worklist is your personal inbox (addressed to you); a Work Queue is a shared team inbox (anyone on the team can grab the next item). Routing is the mailroom deciding which inbox each task goes to.

bulletPoints: Route to a specific user (Worklist) when one person must own the task; route to a Work Queue when any qualified team member can handle it.
Distinguish conditional destinations from Get Next Work’s selection of suitable next work.

elements.description: The sourced Team model describes a primary manager, a shared Work Queue and multiple users, potentially across departments. A user can belong to multiple Work Groups. Authorized managers may transfer work but cannot perform approvals; those outside the group cannot complete its queue tasks.

elements.text: A Work Group is a project team roster; a cross-functional Work Group is a task force pulled from multiple departments so the whole Case can be handled without hand-off delays.

bulletPoints: Work Groups improve efficiency by coordinating users and their shared Work Queues.
In Dev Studio terminology, a Team in App Studio corresponds to a Work Group.

elements.description: An Approve/Reject Step routes to a configured user, queue or business condition and applies configured outcome behavior. Approval may continue/change Stage; rejection may resolve, continue or change Stage. Default rejection is Resolved-Rejected, not necessarily rework.

items: CASCADING — MULTIPLE approvers in sequence (e.g., up a reporting hierarchy or via an authority matrix for higher amounts)

elements.text: Single approval is one signature on the form; cascading approval is a signature chain that climbs the org chart until the amount is fully authorized.

bulletPoints: Cascading approvals can be driven by a reporting structure or an authority matrix (condition-based levels).
Configure outcome behavior; approve and reject do not necessarily take different paths.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Managing Work Deadlines: SLAs and Urgency

elements.description: An SLA defines timing, urgency adjustments, notifications and configured escalations for Case/Stage/Process/Step. Goal and Deadline are measured from the start; repeatable Passed Deadline intervals are measured from the Deadline and configured in Dev Studio.
Two SLA time thresholds on an Assignment or Case:
items: GOAL — the EARLIER target; work SHOULD be completed by this time
DEADLINE — the LATER limit; work MUST be completed by this time

elements.description: Case and Assignment urgency are distinct priorities from 0 to 100. Positive configured increments can raise the relevant urgency at SLA milestones, but do not guarantee completion. At 100 further increments are ignored while configured notifications/escalations still run.

elements.text: Think of urgency as priority rather than automatic completion: attention and escalation still require the configured workflow and available capacity.

bulletPoints: Goal is the desired target; Deadline marks lateness. Both are measured from SLA start.
Urgency affects priority; configured increments stop at 100 without suppressing notifications.
Initial Case urgency is configurable in App Studio Settings > General; initial Assignment adjustments and Passed Deadline settings use Dev Studio.

examPitfalls.title: Worklist vs. Work Queue
examPitfalls.trapDescription: These are routinely swapped. Worklist = one specific user; Work Queue = shared team queue.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: One owner → Worklist (route to a specific user). Any qualified team member → Work Queue.

examPitfalls.title: Goal vs. Deadline direction
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The classic trap: which is earlier. Goal is the EARLIER target (should); Deadline is the LATER limit (must).
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Goal is the desired target and Deadline marks lateness, both measured from the start. Increments occur only as configured.

examPitfalls.title: What Urgency does
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Configured positive urgency adjustments raise priority but do not automatically complete work.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Priority supports timeliness but does not guarantee completion; notifications can still run at urgency 100.

examPitfalls.title: Single vs. cascading approval
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Cascading approval = multiple sequential approvers (hierarchy/authority matrix), not just one.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Multiple levels of sign-off (e.g., by amount) → cascading approval; one approver → single approval.

examPitfalls.title: Cross-functional Work Groups
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Work Groups coordinate users and Work Queues; cross-functional ones span teams to improve efficiency.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Need members from multiple teams on the same work → cross-functional Work Group.

examPitfalls.title: Routing destination choice
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Confusing conditional destination routing with Get Next Work selection by urgency, availability and skills.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use explicit/conditional destinations for routing and Get Next Work for urgency/skill/availability-based work selection.

examPitfalls.title: App Studio vs Dev Studio SLA scope
examPitfalls.trapDescription: App Studio offers goal/deadline; advanced SLA options live in Dev Studio.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Goal/Deadline and initial Case urgency are available in App Studio; initial Assignment adjustments and Passed Deadline configuration use Dev Studio.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An Assignment must be available to any qualified member of the claims team so whoever is free can pick it up. Where should it be routed?

options.text: To a Work Queue (shared team queue)
To a specific user's Worklist
To the customer
To an Access Role

practiceQuiz.hint: A Work Queue is a shared pool where any qualified team member can pull and complete Assignments.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A shared queue fits eligible claims-team work. A named Worklist fixes ownership, an access role defines permissions, and the customer is not the required team destination.

optionExplanations.A: A shared queue allows eligible teammates to pull the work.
optionExplanations.B: A named Worklist fixes ownership instead of allowing the shared pool.
optionExplanations.C: The work belongs to the claims team rather than the customer.
optionExplanations.D: A role describes permissions rather than hold an assignment.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which statement correctly distinguishes a goal from a deadline in an SLA?

options.text: The goal is the earlier target time work should be done; the deadline is the later time work must be done
The deadline is earlier than the goal
Goal and deadline are the same time
The goal is mandatory and the deadline is optional

practiceQuiz.hint: The Goal is the earlier 'should-complete-by' target; the Deadline is the later mandatory limit.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The goal is the earlier 'should complete by' target; the deadline is the later 'must complete by' limit. The goal interval is shorter than the deadline interval.

optionExplanations.A: The goal is the desired target; the deadline marks lateness.
optionExplanations.B: This reverses the requested earlier target and later limit.
optionExplanations.C: The scenario distinguishes two separate milestones.
optionExplanations.D: A goal is not the mandatory cutoff that the deadline represents.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An Assignment has an SLA with positive urgency increments configured at its goal and deadline. What do these urgency adjustments do?

options.text: Increase the Assignment's priority at each configured milestone, up to the urgency limit
It deletes the Case when the deadline passes
It reassigns the Case to the customer
It locks the Ruleset

practiceQuiz.hint: Positive configured adjustments raise priority up to the urgency maximum.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Positive configured increments increase Assignment Urgency at the milestones, up to the maximum of 100. Assignment-level SLAs adjust Assignment Urgency; Case-level SLAs adjust Case Urgency. These are related but distinct priority values.

optionExplanations.A: Configured SLA increments raise the relevant work's priority.
optionExplanations.B: Passing time does not inherently delete the case.
optionExplanations.C: Customer reassignment is not the meaning of urgency.
optionExplanations.D: Ruleset locking is unrelated to work priority.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Expense approvals must be signed off by the submitter's manager and then a director for larger amounts. Which approval pattern is this?

options.text: Cascading approval (multiple sequential approvers via hierarchy/authority matrix)
Single approval
A Work Queue
A duplicate Case search

practiceQuiz.hint: Cascading approval routes through multiple sequential approvers, often based on authority level.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Multiple sequential approvers based on hierarchy or approval amount is cascading approval. A single approval involves only one approver; the other options are unrelated Case features and not approval patterns.

optionExplanations.A: The requirement has multiple ordered approvers.
optionExplanations.B: One approval cannot cover the manager and director chain.
optionExplanations.C: A queue is a routing destination rather than an approval pattern.
optionExplanations.D: Duplicate detection does not obtain the required approvals.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A task must be owned and completed by one specific operator. Where is it routed?

options.text: To that user's Worklist
To a shared Work Queue
To every user in the application
To the Resolution Stage

practiceQuiz.hint: Routing to a named user places the Assignment directly on that operator's personal Worklist.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The named operator’s Worklist fits exclusive ownership. Queue and business-logic routing are also valid alternatives for other requirements; a Stage is not the user destination.

optionExplanations.A: A Worklist gives the named operator assignment ownership.
optionExplanations.B: A shared queue would allow eligible teammates to take it.
optionExplanations.C: Organization-wide assignment does not give one operator ownership.
optionExplanations.D: A lifecycle phase is not the operator's assignment destination.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which capability selects suitable next work using urgency, user availability and skills?

options.text: Configured Get Next Work selection
Always route to the current user
Route to the customer
Disable routing entirely

practiceQuiz.hint: Distinguish work selection from a fixed destination or conditional route.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Get Next Work evaluates those factors when selecting the most suitable Assignment. Conditional routing can choose a destination but is not automatically the same algorithm.

optionExplanations.A: Get Next Work considers urgency, availability and skills for next-work selection.
optionExplanations.B: The current user may lack the required skill or capacity.
optionExplanations.C: The customer is not the qualified service agent described here.
optionExplanations.D: Disabling routing cannot allocate work to the appropriate agent.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is presenting the Work Group concept to a business stakeholder who manages operations across multiple teams. Which TWO statements about Work Groups are correct?

options.text: A Work Group associates users and Work Queues to coordinate work
Cross-functional Work Groups span multiple teams to improve efficiency
A Work Group is the same thing as an Access Role
Work Groups can only contain a single user

practiceQuiz.hint: Work Groups organize users and Work Queues together, and they can span multiple teams or functions.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Work Groups associate users and Work Queues, and cross-functional Work Groups span teams. They are not Access Roles and are not limited to one user. No partial credit.

optionExplanations.A: The group coordinates users and their shared queues.
optionExplanations.B: Cross-functional grouping can coordinate work across team boundaries.
optionExplanations.C: Permission roles and work coordination serve different purposes.
optionExplanations.D: A Work Group can coordinate multiple users.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA configures a goal of 2 hours and a deadline of 8 hours on an Assignment, with positive urgency increments at both milestones. What happens as time passes?

options.text: Urgency increases when the 2-hour goal is reached and again when the 8-hour deadline is reached
The Case is auto-resolved at 2 hours
The deadline is ignored because the goal is shorter
Nothing changes until 24 hours pass

practiceQuiz.hint: The stated positive increments apply at the goal and deadline, up to the limit.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Configured positive Assignment increments apply at two and eight hours up to the urgency maximum. They support priority, not automatic completion or guaranteed order under all other routing constraints.

optionExplanations.A: Positive configured increments apply at the two SLA milestones.
optionExplanations.B: A goal does not automatically resolve the case.
optionExplanations.D: The configured intervals are two and eight hours, not twenty-four.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Where does a BA set the basic goal and deadline, and where are advanced SLA escalations configured?

options.text: Goal/deadline in App Studio; advanced escalations in Dev Studio (the SLA rule)
Both only in Prediction Studio
Both only in Admin Studio
Neither is configurable

practiceQuiz.hint: Basic in App Studio; advanced in Dev Studio.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Goal/Deadline are available in App Studio and Dev Studio. Advanced Passed Deadline settings and initial Assignment adjustments use Dev Studio; initial Case urgency is also configurable in App Studio.

optionExplanations.A: Basic milestones are available in App Studio; advanced SLA work uses Dev Studio.
optionExplanations.B: Prediction Studio handles analytical models rather than these timing rules.
optionExplanations.C: Admin Studio monitoring is not the authoring surface for both settings.
optionExplanations.D: The platform provides configurable service-level behavior.

practiceQuiz.scenario: In Dev Studio terminology, what is the App Studio 'goal and deadline' called?

options.text: A Service-Level Agreement (SLA)
A Property
An Operator
A Work Group

practiceQuiz.hint: In App Studio the pair of Goal and Deadline is what Dev Studio calls a Service Level Agreement (SLA).
practiceQuiz.rationale: Goal and deadline in App Studio correspond to the Service-Level Agreement (SLA) rule in Dev Studio. The others map to Field, User, and Team respectively.

optionExplanations.A: The service-level rule defines the timing milestones.
optionExplanations.B: A property holds a value rather than define this timing policy.
optionExplanations.C: An operator represents a user rather than the timing rule.
optionExplanations.D: A Work Group coordinates teams rather than name this policy.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA configures Reject to resolve a loan application. What happens when the approver rejects it?

options.text: The configured rejection handling resolves the Case, with its configured rejection status
It is permanently deleted
It is routed to the customer's Worklist
Nothing changes; approve and reject behave identically

practiceQuiz.hint: Follow the configured Reject outcome, not an assumed rework branch.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Reject behavior can resolve, continue or change Stage. This scenario explicitly configures resolution; the documented default status is Resolved-Rejected.

optionExplanations.A: The configured Reject outcome controls resolution and status.
optionExplanations.B: Rejection does not inherently delete the submitted case.
optionExplanations.C: Routing to a customer is not a universal rejection behavior.
optionExplanations.D: The outcomes can explicitly follow different paths.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which TWO are valid reasons to route an Assignment to a Work Queue rather than a specific user?

options.text: Any qualified member of the team can perform the work
Work should be pulled by whoever becomes available next
Only one named person is allowed to ever do it
The work must be hidden from the entire team

practiceQuiz.hint: A Work Queue is the shared, pull-based construct for team-based Assignment routing.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Work Queues suit shared, pull-based work any qualified member can take. A single mandatory owner indicates a Worklist, and hiding work from the team is not a routing goal. No partial credit.

optionExplanations.A: Shared ownership lets any eligible teammate perform the task.
optionExplanations.B: Pulling by availability fits a team queue.
optionExplanations.C: Exclusive named ownership instead fits that person's Worklist.
optionExplanations.D: A queue destination does not implement hiding from every team member.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is the primary business value of assignment routing and approvals as workflow-automation features?

options.text: They orchestrate work across teams and ensure the right people complete the right work efficiently and on time
They eliminate the need for any users
They replace the Case Life Cycle
They store data in external systems

practiceQuiz.hint: Routing and approvals ensure the right work reaches the right person at the right time.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Routing and approvals orchestrate cross-team work by getting the right Assignments to the right operators efficiently and supporting on-time, governed completion. They are foundational to structured business process management.

optionExplanations.A: Routing and approval coordinate responsibility and decision points.
optionExplanations.B: The described steps still involve people completing work.
optionExplanations.C: These features operate within the lifecycle rather than replace it.
optionExplanations.D: External persistence is an integration concern rather than the main value here.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is explaining to a business user how a single Approve/Reject Step affects Case routing in a workflow. Which option best describes how a single approval step interacts with the Case flow?

options.text: One approver decides approve/reject, and the outcome routes the Case forward or to rework
Every user in the org must approve before proceeding
Approvals never affect the Case path
Approvals are only decorative

practiceQuiz.hint: A single approval involves exactly one approver whose decision (approve/reject) determines the next path.
practiceQuiz.rationale: One approver makes the decision and the configured outcome behavior determines what happens next. Distinct approve/reject decisions do not require different paths in every configuration.

optionExplanations.A: The configured outcome determines continuation or rework.
optionExplanations.B: A single approval does not require organization-wide signoff.
optionExplanations.C: Approval results can change the workflow path.
optionExplanations.D: The decision is functional rather than decorative.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Why might a BA choose a Worklist over a Work Queue for a sensitive compliance review?

options.text: Because a specific, accountable individual must own and complete the review
Because no one should ever see it
Because Work Queues cannot hold Assignments
Because Worklists are faster to delete

practiceQuiz.hint: Assigning work to a specific named user creates direct accountability with one designated owner.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A Worklist assigns work to a specific accountable owner, appropriate when one named individual must complete a sensitive task. Work Queues can hold Assignments (shared); the other options are false.

optionExplanations.A: Named ownership provides the required accountability.
optionExplanations.B: Assignment ownership is not the same as visibility restrictions.
optionExplanations.C: Queues can hold assignments for shared work.
optionExplanations.D: Deletion speed is unrelated to review accountability.

quickRecap.value: Explicit/conditional user or queue destinations differ from Get Next Work’s urgency/availability/skill selection.
Associate users and Work Queues; cross-functional Work Groups span teams to improve efficiency. (Team in App Studio = Work Group in Dev Studio.)
Single (one approver) vs. cascading (multiple sequential approvers via hierarchy/authority matrix); approve/reject routes the Case.
Goal desired target and Deadline lateness threshold are measured from SLA start; Passed Deadline repeats from Deadline.
Case/Assignment priorities 0–100; configured increments support timeliness, not guarantee it. Notifications can still run at 100.
Initial Case urgency is available in App Studio; initial Assignment and Passed Deadline settings use Dev Studio.
